sentences.text: Good afternoon Delphine, thanks for the time.
I have Tom Bradshaw with me, he is one of our solutions consultants and he knows the learning side far better than I do.
The plan for today is that you talk and we listen, and towards the end Tom will show you two or three things if they seem relevant.
Good afternoon to you both.
That suits me. I have sat through a number of presentations this year, so questions make a change.
Hello Delphine. I will mostly be quiet until Priya has got what she needs.
Start wherever you like. What does the society actually do, and who for?
We are the professional body for arborists across five states in the upper midwest.
About seven thousand members, of whom roughly four thousand five hundred hold a certification that has to be maintained.
Maintaining it means a set number of education units every three years, and we are the ones who deliver and record most of those units.
So the education programme is not an extra for you, it is the reason people are members.
It is the whole proposition, yes.
If somebody lets their certification lapse they are off the approved contractor lists in three states, and that is their income gone.
So the stakes for the individual member are high, which means the stakes for us are high.
How are you delivering the education today?
Three ways. In person workshops at regional chapters, which is about forty a year.
Live online sessions, which grew enormously in the last few years and are now about sixty a year.
And self paced courses, which is about ninety four titles at the moment.
Tell me about the chapter structure, because you mentioned five states and I want to understand how independent they are.
Each state chapter has its own board, its own treasurer and its own bank account, and they remit a share of dues to the national body.
The national body holds the certification, the standards and the education programme, and the chapters hold the local events and the social side.
It is a federation rather than branches, and anybody who forgets that finds out quickly at the annual meeting.
How much of the administration happens at the chapter level?
Quite a lot of it. Each chapter keeps its own event records and three of the five keep their own spreadsheets of who attended what.
Two of the five have a paid part time administrator and three rely entirely on a volunteer treasurer.
The national office reconciles the five sets of records at the end of every year, and that takes about six weeks.
Does that reconciliation feed the certification records, or is it purely financial?
Both. A chapter workshop carries education units, so the chapter record feeds the certification record as well as the accounts.
The certification board reviews a sample of those records every year and it has reviewed ours twice since I arrived.
They give us six weeks of notice and they tell us which sample they have drawn.
So the national record and the five chapter records are separate things today.
They are, yes. The board paper I wrote describes them as one thing, which was optimistic of me.
I have been rewriting that paragraph for a fortnight.
Understood. What is the current relationship between the chapters and whatever systems they use?
There is none to speak of. Five chapters, five sets of tools, and a national office that receives spreadsheets by email twice a year.
I have been here three years and the national systems sit in my remit, which is how I ended up running this.
Tell us about the self paced courses. What are they built in at the moment?
They are built by two different vendors who specialise in technical safety training.
One of them produces course packages in an industry standard format, and the other one does too, because that is what everyone in safety training produces.
We have ninety four of those courses and we add about a dozen a year.
And where do they live now?
On a hosted platform we have used for eleven years, which is being retired by its owner next September.
That deadline is the reason we are having this conversation at all, and it is the reason I am talking to four vendors rather than none.
That is a helpful piece of context to have early.
So the requirement is not simply a learning system, it is somewhere those ninety four existing courses can live without being rebuilt.
Correct, and I want to be very direct about this because it has already ended one conversation with another vendor.
We need to upload SCORM 1.2 and SCORM 2004 packages straight into the learning module without rebuilding every course by hand.
If that is not possible then nothing else you show me matters, because rebuilding ninety four courses is a two year project and we have twelve months.
That is a fair way to put it and I would rather you put it that way now than in three months.
Let me ask two clarifying questions so that my answer is useful rather than reassuring.
Are the packages single course files, or are some of them larger collections with multiple modules inside?
Both. About sixty are single courses. The rest are collections, and the largest one has eleven modules inside it.
The eleven modules were authored in a fixed order and that is the order they are stored in.
And how is a completion recorded against a member today, once somebody finishes one of those courses?
The hosted platform writes completion, score and time spent to a file, and our membership clerk keys those three numbers onto the member record once a week.
The time spent figure surprises people, but the board sets a minimum time for some units regardless of how fast somebody clicks through.
That is clear, thank you. I will note how that flows today so that the written answer covers it.
Beyond the courses themselves, what else does the national office run day to day?
Member records and dues, because the certification and the membership are the same thing for us.
The chapter structure, because our five state chapters each run their own budget and their own events.
And the quarterly return to the certification board, which today is one person exporting to a spreadsheet for two days.
Who is the certification board, in terms of how much say they have over your choices?
They are a national body and they have a great deal of say.
They do not tell us what software to buy, but they do tell us what records we have to be able to produce on demand, and the practical effect is much the same.
Let me ask about dues and the money side, since your chapters hold their own accounts.
How does that actually work today?
A member pays one amount to the national body. We keep sixty percent and remit forty to their chapter quarterly.
Dues are one hundred and eighty dollars a year for a certified member, ninety for an associate and forty five for a student.
That gives us about one point one million in dues income, against a total income of about two point six million once education and the annual meeting are counted.
And the remittance to the chapters, how is that calculated and checked?
By our finance manager, in a spreadsheet, four times a year, over about three days each time.
She has done it since 2014 and she retires in two years.
She keeps the workings in the same spreadsheet every quarter and the file goes to our auditors with the year end pack.
And who sees those numbers today, outside the finance office?
The chapter treasurers see their own line when she sends the quarterly statement, and the executive director sees the total.
Nobody looks at it in between, because there is nothing to look at until she runs it.
Understood. Have you been through a change of this kind before?
I have been through one system replacement in a previous role, at a trade association about half our size.
It took fourteen months end to end and I learned a great deal about sequencing from it.
Understood. What does your decision process look like between now and the deadline?
We are talking to four vendors through September.
Two go forward to a proper evaluation in October, which will involve our education committee and two of the chapter chairs.
A recommendation to the board in December, a decision in January, and then eight months to move everything.
Eight months to move ninety four courses, seven thousand member records and five chapter structures is tight but it is not unreasonable.
Who else is in the room for the October evaluation?
Our education committee, which is six people and meets monthly.
Two chapter chairs, chosen by rotation, and they are the ones who know how the treasurers work.
And our executive director, who joins for the second half.
What does your procurement actually require of us? I would rather know now than be surprised in November.
We are a nonprofit rather than a public body, so there is no formal tender requirement, but our own policy says three written quotations above one hundred thousand dollars over the term.
The paperwork that goes with that is a written proposal, a five year cost, two references from organisations of a similar size, and a security questionnaire.
The security part is new this year and it came from our insurer rather than from us.
What form does the insurer want the security evidence in?
A completed questionnaire, about sixty questions, and whatever independent assessment you hold.
I have sent it to the other three vendors already and two of them have returned it, so it is not an unusual ask.
I will send it to you this evening so that it is not sitting on the critical path in November.
Please do, and I will get it back inside two weeks.
On the references, would you rather speak to an organisation with a similar certification obligation, or one of a similar size?
Certification obligation, every time. Size I can imagine on my own. A board that reviews our records is a particular kind of pressure and it is useful to hear from somebody who works under one.
Then that is who I will offer you, and I will ask them first rather than giving you a name and hoping.
Thank you. One of the other vendors gave me three names who had not been warned, and two of them were plainly irritated to hear from me.
Then let me answer your first question now, since it decides whether the rest is worth your time.

On the package formats you named, I want to check one detail on the collections that have several modules inside them before I give you a yes, so I am going to confirm that in writing tomorrow rather than say something loose on a call.
Everything else you have described, including completion, score and time spent going back onto the member record, is standard for us.
I would rather have that answer tomorrow in writing than today out loud, so that works well.
Send it with the five year cost while you are at it and you will have saved our executive director an email.
We will do both.
Written answer on the course packages from Tom tomorrow, and an indicative five year cost from me by the end of the week, clearly marked indicative.
Would a longer session with your education committee in early October be useful?
It would, assuming tomorrow's answer is the one I am expecting.
Let us leave that hanging until then rather than book something I might have to cancel.
That is sensible. Thank you Delphine, this has been a genuinely useful hour.
Thank you both. Speak tomorrow.
